questions.explain: RPO is the maximum acceptable data loss measured in time (drives backup frequency), while RTO is the maximum acceptable time to restore service (drives backup storage, warm standby, and restore complexity).
options: RPO measures restore time and RTO measures data loss
They are synonyms for the same metric
RPO is the maximum acceptable data loss measured in time; RTO is the maximum acceptable time to restore service
RPO only applies to differential backups
questions.q: What is the difference between RPO and RTO, and what does each one drive?

questions.explain: A differential captures everything changed since the last full backup (tracked by the differential bitmap), so restore needs exactly two files: the last full and the latest differential.
options: The last full backup plus every differential since
The last full backup plus only the latest differential
Only the latest differential by itself
The full backup plus all log backups since Sunday
questions.q: To restore a database using a differential backup, which files are required?

questions.explain: The chapter calls it a common and dangerous mistake: until that first full backup, SQL Server cannot form a log chain and the database behaves like SIMPLE mode — no point-in-time recovery.
options: The database behaves like SIMPLE mode until the first full backup is taken, because no log chain can form
The differential bitmap is cleared
BACKUP LOG fails permanently
The database becomes read-only
questions.q: What happens if you switch a database to the FULL recovery model but do not take a full backup afterward?

questions.explain: WITH COPY_ONLY takes a full or log backup without affecting the differential baseline or log chain — ideal for one-off backups like pre-deployment snapshots.
options: It produces a smaller compressed backup
It encrypts the backup automatically
It skips the differential bitmap
It leaves the regular backup schedule and log chain undisturbed, making it safe for one-off backups
questions.q: What is the purpose of WITH COPY_ONLY on a BACKUP DATABASE command?

questions.explain: The chapter states: an untested backup is not a backup. RESTORE VERIFYONLY checks structural integrity without restoring; DBCC CHECKDB after a test restore verifies actual data pages; runbooks should be written before incidents.
options: Monitoring that backup jobs complete successfully
RESTORE VERIFYONLY only, since it performs a full restore
An untested backup is not a backup — schedule full test restores, validate with RESTORE VERIFYONLY and DBCC CHECKDB, and build runbooks in advance
Checking the msdb.dbo.backupset table daily
